title: US forced-labor tariff to figure in Marcos-Trump talks
summary: The Philippines wants the 12.5% duty on covered exports reduced.

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump greets Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the White House on July 22, 2025 in Washington, DC.

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and United States President Donald Trump are expected to take up in their talks on Wednesday, November 18, the US' standing 12.5% tariff on Philippine exports.

Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said on Monday, November 16, the two leaders will discuss during their bilateral engagement the duty imposed by the US on the Philippines in July over allegations that Manila was doing little to prevent the entry of imports made with forced labor.

At a press briefing before the start of the second day of the 49th ASEAN Summit, Roque said US officials had already received the joint administrative order (JAO) the Philippine government issued to bar such imports, though she did not say whether or how Washington had responded.
"They have already received the JAO and we will be discussing actually on November 18, all of this," Roque told reporters.
Asked what message the Philippines would bring to the talks, Roque said: "I cannot disclose it now, so it's best for us to wait for November 18."
"Of course my wish is to bring down the tariffs. We want to expand the exports to the US and to all other markets globally," Roque told reporters.
Trump is due to land in Manila on Tuesday afternoon, November 17, after the main summit sessions end and Marcos hands the bloc's rotating chairship to Singapore.
Marcos will receive Trump at Malacañang Palace on Wednesday before the US leader flies on to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Washington imposed the duty on July 24 after a Section 301 investigation by the Office of the US Trade Representative concluded that the Philippines had "failed to impose and effectively enforce a forced-labor import prohibition."

Economies that already banned such imports, or had committed to do so in trade agreements with Washington, received a lower 10-percent rate, among them Indonesia and Malaysia. The Philippines landed in the 12.5% group along with Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The Department of Trade and Industry earlier estimated about 34% of Philippine exports to the United States, worth roughly $6.25 billion based on 2025 data, would be subject to the higher duty.

The Trump administration had turned to investigations into alleged forced labor in March after the US Supreme Court struck down the sweeping tariffs Trump imposed under an emergency powers law. Those initial tariffs include the 19% "reciprocal" rate Marcos negotiated with Trump at the White House in a July 2025 visit.

"We have already released a joint administrative order last month on the forced labor... We do not do forced labor here in the Philippines. We are very firm that there is no forced labor and no child labor here in the Philippines," Roque said.

The JAO signed in July created an inter-agency committee chaired by the DTI to receive and investigate complaints about imported goods suspected of being made wholly or partly with forced labor, and to recommend action against them.
